background.definition: Chronic venous insufficiency (CVI) occurs from abnormally functioning venous system of the lower extremities with venous hypertension that causes edema, skin changes, and ulcerations.

list.listitem: In the United States, approximately 150,000 new cases of venous insufficiency occur each year.
Approximately 2.5 million people have CVI in the United States.
Depending on risk factors and whether the population studied is in a referral center, estimates of US prevalence of CVI range from 1% to 40% for women and 1% to 17% for men.
Valvular incompetence in either superficial or deep venous system
Deep venous thrombosis (venous obstruction)
Failure of the pumping effect of leg muscles on venous flow
Venous hypertension is the main mechanism responsible for CVI.
Reflux through incompetent valves, failure of the calf muscle pumping function, and venous outflow obstruction cause venous hypertension.
The excess volume and pressure resulting from valve incompetence eventually distends both the deep and superficial veins. The abnormally distended veins further worsen valvular incompetence.
High pressures generated by calf muscle contractions in deep veins are transmitted to superficial veins and capillaries, which is normally decreased by competent values.
Prolonged venous hypertension causes histologic changes in the capillary system, resulting in increased permeability to various substances, triggering inflammation.
A fibrin cuff is formed in the surrounding tissues from the leaked fibrinogen. Ultimately, the interstitial edema and fibrin causes tissue hypoxia.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: History of deep venous thrombosis or phlebitis

list.listitem: The clinical manifestations range from asymptomatic presentation to more pronounced skin changes, including varicose veins, edema, skin changes, and venous ulceration.

Dilated veins, including telangiectases (dilated intradermal venules less than 1 mm in size), reticular veins (dilated, nonpalpable subdermal veins less than or equal to 4 mm in size), and varicose veins (dilated, palpable subcutaneous veins larger than 4 mm), occur in 5% to 15% of patients.
Leg discomfort can present as dull ache, pain, pressure, or heaviness in the legs.
Leg edema, usually suggesting more advanced disease than just venous dilation, occurs in 5% to 20% of patients.

Skin changes include eczema, brownish discoloration, erythema, signs of active or prior ulcers, and lipodermatosclerosis (fibrosis of skin and subcutaneous tissues along with fat necrosis) suggest more severe venous disease. These occur in up to 10% of patients.
Venous ulceration typically are located around the medial malleolus or along the saphenous venous distribution.

In a prospective study of 342 consecutive patients with varicose veins at a vascular clinic, clinical suspicion of CVI by experienced surgeons was only 32% sensitive and 77% specific compared with venous duplex scanning.
Chronic pelvic pain can be a manifestation of pelvic venous insufficiency.
A clinical diagnosis of CVI is unreliable; diagnostic imaging is required to confirm the diagnosis and also to determine the etiology.
Work up patients with risk factors or symptoms or signs suggesting peripheral vascular disease.

Duplex ultrasonography is the test of choice in evaluating the morphology and hemodynamics of the lower extremity veins and has replaced venography. Venous photoplethysmography (PPG) and air plethysmography (APG) measure volume changes in the legs and are also used to evaluate CVI.

Duplex ultrasonography is more accurate than PPG or APG in the diagnosis of long saphenous incompetence (sensitivity = 73%; specificity = 85%), but is relatively insensitive in detecting deep vein reflux (sensitivity = 48%). PPG is more accurate than ultrasound in detecting deep vein reflux (sensitivity = 79%; specificity = 70%).
Duplex ultrasonography is more sensitive (77% vs 55%) and more specific (85% vs 41%) than venography for predicting severe venous insufficiency.
Patients with CVI should be treated with compression stockings.

When compression stockings are ineffective at reducing symptoms, reducing swelling, or preventing or healing venous ulcers, patients should undergo noninvasive testing to elucidate the etiology and to guide management.
There are limited studies examining non-pharmacological strategies for the prevention of venous insufficiency in a standing worker population.
There are limited clinical trials comparing compression versus no compression in patients with CVI and recurrent leg ulcers, but compression stockings represent the mainstay of management. C
For patients not responding to compression stockings, endoscopic perforator vein ligation, venous valvuloplasty, and external vein ligation are all effective. A
Topical steroids provide short-term improvement in stasis dermatitis.B
The main active compound of HCSE in a dose of 50 to 75 mg twice daily is an effective treatment for CVI. In a systematic review, 6 of 7 studies found a reduction of leg pain in the HCSE group. A
There is insufficient evidence to support the routine use of systemic antibiotics for venous leg ulcers.

Medications are generally not used in the treatment of CVI. A Cochrane review of phlebotonics such as rutosides, hidrosmine and diosmine, calcium dobesilate, and pine bark extract found a small reduction in ankle circumference (˜0.5 cm) compared with placebo but no effect on quality of life.

As many as 80% of patients with recurrent venous thromboembolic events have venous insufficiency. If 100 patients with second episodes of deep venous thrombosis/pulmonary embolism were treated with oral anticoagulants indefinitely instead of for 6 months, 1 episode of recurrent thromboembolism would be prevented every 2.5 months (NNT for 1 year to prevent 1 episode = 19.4) at a cost of 1 major hemorrhage every 5 months.
Patients with venous stasis ulcers may benefit from adjunctive therapy with aspirin, pentoxiphylline, or intravenous iloprost.
Anabolic steroids such as stanozolol in conjunction with compression therapy may be helpful in treating lipodermatosclerosis of the lower extremities.
Topical steroids have been shown to provide short-term improvement in stasis dermatitis.
There is no evidence to suggest that routine use of systemic antibiotics promotes healing of venous ulcers.
A small study randomized 65 participants to crisaborole ointment 2% (a non-steroidal PDE4 inhibitor) or vehicle cream. It was judged to be effective but longer and larger studies are needed.
A Cochrane review of randomized trials of patients with CVI, ligation and valvuloplasty concluded that they produce comparable long-term improvement in symptoms.

A network meta-analysis compared endovenous therapies in patients with saphenous vein insufficiency. They concluded that cyanoacrylate adhesive closure had the lowest 6 week rate of treatment failure, radiofrequency ablation had the greatest improvement in symptoms, and high ligation with stripping that the lowest rate of long-term recurrence.

In a systematic review that included case series and other observational designs, the overall complication rate was 11%. Short term wound healing was 99.9% for ultrasound guided sclerotherapy, 72% for open ligation, and 96% for subfascial endoscopic perforator surgery (SEPS). Wound recurrence was 9% with SEPS.

Endovenous laser ablation treatment in a randomized trial led to similar outcomes at five years as endovenous laser therapy with ambulatory phlebectomy. A Cochrane review concluded that there is insufficient evidence to conclude the effectivness of surgical intervention on deep venous insufficiency.

An adequately powered Dutch study randomized 464 patients with an incompetent great saphenous vein or an anterior accesssory saphenous vein with one or more incompetent branches to a single ambulatory phlebectomy (SAC) or to thermal endovenous ablation with concomitant phlebectomy (TAP). At one year SAC was non-inferior to TAP and was more cost-effective.

A UK study randomized 167 patients with primary truncal vein incompetence to mechanochemical ablation (MOCA) or cyanoacrylate adhesive injection (CAI). Outcomes were similar with regards to symptom improvement, post-procedure pain, and disease specific quality of life.

The main active compound of horse chestnut seed extract (HCSE) is aescin, and in a dose of 50 to 75 mg twice daily is an effective treatment for CVI. The side effects of aescin are mild and infrequent.

HCSE decreases leg pain in nearly two-thirds of patients compared with less than half of patients taking placebo (NNT = 6; 95% CI, 4-10), with a mean reduction of 4 mm on a 100-mm visual analog scale. HCSE also demonstrates comparable decreases in edema (NNT = 4; 95% CI, 3-7).

The data on the effectiveness of other phlebotonic agents (rutosides, hidrosmine, diosmine, calcium dobesilate, chromocarbe, centella asiatica, disodium flavodate, french maritime pine bark extract, grape seed extract, and aminaftone) are too limited to recommend their use.

A systematic review of 8 studies including 5 RCTs found some benefits in terms of ankle and calf circumference as well as subjective feeling of swelling for oral micronized purified flavonoid fraction (Diosmin and Hesperidin). Studies were heterogeneous and of mixed quality.
A systematic review found limited support for red vine leaf extract although based on low quality evidence.
Existing studies fail to support the benefit of hyperbaric oxygen for chronic venous insufficienty.
For patients with mild venous insufficiency, leg elevation alone may be sufficient.

Although there are limited studies comparing compression versus no compression in patients with CVI and recurrent leg ulcers, compression stockings represent the mainstay of management. There is insufficient evidence to support recommendation of such non-pharmacologic therapy for prevention of CVI in standing workers.

Clinical trials comparing high levels of compression with medium levels show comparable rates of preventing ulcers, but only one third of patients using medium-level compression stockings stopped using them compared with nearly half the patients using high-level compression stockings. If patients can tolerate the stockings, there may be some benefit.In patients with ulcers, compression stocking improve healing rates when compared to no compression.
There is no clear evidence to suggest on type of stocking or length is superior.
A limitation of compression is low rates of adherence. A review identified physical limitations, poor health literacy, cost, discomfort and psychosocial issues as barriers.
Intermittent pneumatic compression therapy may increase wound healing when compared to no compression, but its value over compression stocking is unclear.
Compression therapy is contraindicated in patients with peripheral arterial disease.
There is insufficient evidence to support ultrasound therapy for the treatment of venous ulcers.

A Cochrane review found 5 RCTs with only 146 participants comparing physical exercise with no exercise for CVI. The authors were unable to draw any conclusions about the benefit of exercise in this limited evidence base.

A Cochrane review of 9 RCTs with 1126 participants concluded that balneotherapy likely improves disease severity scores slightly (moderate certainty evidence), that it reduces pain and skin pigmentation changes (low certainty), and improves health related quality of life (very low certainty).
The most common complication is venous stasis ulcer. See that chapter for management.
The prognosis is usually good in the absence of other comorbid conditions that also cause leg swelling. C
Most patients with uncomplicated disease respond well to outpatient therapy and follow-up. C

Permanent changes of the affected areas can include fibrosis and hemosiderosis. Skin and soft tissue injury continues in the absence of cutaneous support, such as compression therapy. Loss of valvular function is irreversible. C
External compression stockings do not appear to have any advantages in reducing edema in pregnant women.
Rutosides may help to relieve the symptoms of varicose veins in late pregnancy, but this is only based on one study and safety evidence is not adequate.
